extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, regulated parties, and agency staff seeking guidance on California rulemaking and OAL procedures
extracted.subtask_description: FAQ guidance about California Administrative Procedure Act (APA) rulemaking procedures, OAL's role, timelines, publications, and how members of the public may participate or petition agencies. Focused on practical procedural standards for notice-and-comment and emergency rulemaking in California.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and standards of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 3.5 of the APA establishes rulemaking procedures and standards for state agencies in California. The requirements set forth in the APA are designed to provide the public with a meaningful opportunity to participate in the adoption of state regulations and to ensure that regulations are clear, necessary and legally valid. The APA is found in the California Government Code, commencing with section 11340. State regulations must also be adopted in compliance with regulations adopted by OAL (California Code of Regulations, title 1, sections 1-120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA is the governing statutory standard: public participation, clarity, necessity, and legal validity are explicit evaluative criteria for regulations; agencies must also follow OAL's Title 1 CCR rules when adopting regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to send comments on proposed regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL cannot accept comments on proposed regulations. Comments on proposed regulations must go directly to the agency which is proposing them during the public comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: For emergency regulations you may comment both directly to the agency and to OAL within a specified period, unless the emergency situation clearly poses such an immediate, serious harm that delaying action to allow public comment would be inconsistent with the public interest. (Government Code sections 11346.1(a)(3) and 11349.6(b) and Title 1, CCR, section 55.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency rulemaking process characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of rulemaking procedures: regular or emergency. The Emergency Rulemaking Process has different requirements but generally include a brief public notice period, a brief public comment period, review by OAL and an OAL decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some agencies may have unique requirements. The APA standards and procedures for emergency regulations were revised effective January 1, 2007 (AB 1302). For more, consult OAL’s Emergency Rulemaking Process page or contact the OAL Reference Attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL's limitation on providing legal advice
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL does not provide legal advice. OAL can answer questions on the statutes and regulations governing California rulemakings and the status of regulations filed with OAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL cannot answer legal matters unrelated to the APA. For legal problems, contact local Bar Association lawyer referral services or the State Bar Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and purposes of OAL publications (CCR, CCR Supplement/Register, Notice Register)
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL publishes: (1) the California Code of Regulations (CCR); (2) the California Code of Regulations Supplement (CCR Supplement); and (3) the California Regulatory Notice Register (Notice Register). The CCR contains regulations duly adopted pursuant to the APA. After OAL approves a proposed regulation, it files the regulation with the Secretary of State. The CCR Supplement (Register) updates the hard copy publication weekly; the online CCR is updated weekly electronically. The Notice Register is the weekly publication of agencies’ Notices of Adoption, Amendment, or Repeal of regulations and other rulemaking activity information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these publications to locate current and recent regulatory text and notice information; the Notice Register includes announcements and is the source for current rulemaking activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find the California Code of Regulations (CCR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCR is available online, at County Clerks, County Law Libraries, and state depository libraries. It is available in loose-leaf form from the publisher, Thomson-Reuters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For loose-leaf copies or publisher information contact Thomson Reuters at 1-888-728-7677.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find the California Code of Regulations Supplement (Register)
rubrics_metrics.description: The California State Law Library houses a collection of past CCR Supplements (Registers) going back to 1945 in various media formats. OAL keeps a set but is limited in media formats and cannot offer public library/research services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the Witkin State Law Library (address, phone, fax, email provided) for research assistance and access to historical Registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find the California Regulatory Notice Register
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL’s California Regulatory Notice Register (‘Notice Register’) page provides the online weekly Notice Register, subscription information and an archive going back several years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OAL’s Notice Register page for current notices and archival research of agency rulemaking notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL review timeline for regular rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, OAL has 30 working days to approve or disapprove a regulation after it has been submitted to OAL for review. (Government Code section 11349.3.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekends and state holidays are excluded from counting this 30 working day period.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL review timeline for emergency rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL has 10 calendar days to approve or disapprove an emergency regulation after it has been submitted to OAL for review. (Government Code section 11349.6.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counting calendar days, weekends and state holidays are not excluded unless they fall on the last day of the review period. Example provided illustrating exclusion of weekends if they fall before the last day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between OAL and OAH
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL is not the same as the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH). OAL carries out the rulemaking part of the APA; OAH is a quasi-judicial tribunal that hears administrative disputes and provides adjudication and alternative dispute resolution services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL does not conduct administrative hearings; OAH handles license revocation hearings and other APA-style adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes an administrative or rulemaking agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The California Constitution and statutes create state agencies, departments, offices, commissions, boards, etc., to carry out laws. These state agencies exercise powers granted by statute or constitution which often include rulemaking (the making of rules and regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies exercise rulemaking only to the extent of authority granted by statute/constitution; their rulemaking power derives from those enabling laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between a regulation and a statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legislature (and the People) enact statutes. Administrative agencies adopt, amend and repeal regulations under authority granted by statutes or constitutional provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the Legislature has created an exemption, agencies must follow the procedures in the APA when adopting, amending or repealing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL does not review statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: No. OAL does not review statutes enacted by the Legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL's review jurisdiction is limited to regulations adopted by agencies under the APA, not statutory enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to petition an agency to change regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: You may ask an agency to repeal or amend an existing regulation, or to adopt a new regulation by petitioning the agency, using the method described in Government Code sections 11340.6 and 11340.7. A petition is simply a letter that requests the change and contains certain information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must identify the nature of the regulation change, the reason for the request, and the agency’s rulemaking power (a reference to the law giving the agency the power to adopt rules and regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligations after receiving a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: By law, the agency must notify you in writing of the receipt and any denial of the petition within 30 calendar days. Any denial must be in writing and include the reasons the agency reached its decision. If the agency does not deny the petition it must schedule the matter for a public hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any decision denying or granting a petition, in whole or in part, must be in writing and transmitted to OAL for publication in the Notice Register. The agency may take other action it determines necessary but must notify the petitioner in writing of any such action. See Government Code sections 11340.6 and 11340.7 for the full petition process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding past versions of a regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a past version of a regulation or research its history, please see Finding Past Versions of a Regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL provides (or links to) resources for historical research of regulatory text; consult the referenced page for procedures and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic submissions and related FAQs
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL provides frequently asked questions regarding Electronic Submissions and a link to that content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult OAL’s Electronic Submissions FAQ for standards, formats, and procedures for submitting materials electronically to OAL (page linked).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to receive notice of proposed rulemakings by OAL
rubrics_metrics.description: If you wish to receive notice of proposed rulemakings by OAL, send an email to oalproposedrulemakings@oal.ca.gov and request to be put on OAL's mailing list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mailing list to receive timely notice of OAL's proposed rulemaking activity.
